title: CompTIA Core: A+ / Network+ / Security+
tagline: The trifecta — hardware, networking, security basics

scenarios.title: No display, but the fans are spinning
scenarios.situation: A workstation powers on: fans spin, drive light flickers, but the monitor stays black and the speaker emits a repeating beep pattern.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best FIRST troubleshooting step?
choices: Reseat the RAM modules and note the beep-code pattern against the motherboard manual
Replace the motherboard immediately
Reinstall the operating system
Swap the power supply for a higher-wattage unit
scenarios.why: Beep codes plus fans-with-no-video point to a POST failure before the OS ever loads — most often RAM seating or a dead stick. Reseating RAM is fast, free, and reversible, and the beep pattern identifies the failing component.
scenarios.hint: What does the motherboard check before it ever touches the disk?

scenarios.title: Shutdowns under heavy load
scenarios.situation: A desktop runs fine for office work but powers off without warning during video renders. The system log shows thermal events just before each shutdown, and the exhaust air feels very hot.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: Dried thermal paste and dust-clogged heatsink — clean the cooler and reapply paste
Underpowered PSU — install a bigger one
Too little RAM — add another stick
Corrupt GPU drivers — reinstall them
scenarios.why: Thermal events before shutdown mean the CPU is overheating and triggering its protection cutoff. Dust insulates the heatsink and old paste stops transferring heat; cleaning and repasting restores cooling. A PSU or driver issue would not log thermal events.
scenarios.hint: What builds up between a CPU and its cooler over the years?

scenarios.title: Two drives, one requirement: survive a disk failure
scenarios.situation: A small office is building a 2-bay NAS for shared files. Their one hard requirement is that a single drive failure must not lose data.
scenarios.prompt: Which RAID level meets the requirement with two disks?
choices: RAID 1
RAID 0
RAID 5
JBOD / spanning
scenarios.why: RAID 1 mirrors identical data to both disks, so either disk alone keeps the array alive. RAID 0 stripes with zero redundancy, RAID 5 needs at least three disks, and JBOD offers no protection at all.
scenarios.hint: Which level writes the exact same data to both disks?

scenarios.title: The swelling battery
scenarios.situation: A user's laptop trackpad has started lifting from below, and the bottom case bulges. The battery is visibly swollen.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Power it off, stop using it, and replace/recycle it through a proper e-waste channel
Puncture the battery to release the trapped gas
Keep using it, but only on AC power with the battery removed by the user prying it out
Put it in the freezer to shrink the swelling
scenarios.why: A swollen lithium-ion battery is a fire and chemical hazard. It must not be punctured, charged, or thrown in the trash; power down, handle gently, and recycle via e-waste. Puncturing or freezing it risks thermal runaway.
scenarios.hint: What is inside a lithium battery that you never want exposed to air?

scenarios.title: Ghost images down the page
scenarios.situation: A laser printer repeats a faint copy of the same image further down every page. The paper path is clear and the driver is current.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: Worn imaging drum or depleted toner cartridge — replace the consumable
Empty paper tray sensor misreading
Outdated printer driver
Dusty exterior vents
scenarios.why: Ghosting on a laser printer means the drum is not fully discharging between rotations or toner is low, so a faint residual image transfers again. It is a consumable problem, not software — the driver cannot cause a repeated physical image.
scenarios.hint: Which part holds the electrostatic image just before toner transfers to the page?

scenarios.title: Works on one PC, not another
scenarios.situation: A USB flash drive works fine on the user's home PC but shows as an unknown device on the office workstation. Other USB devices work on that workstation.
scenarios.prompt: What should you try first?
choices: Plug it into a rear motherboard USB port and reinstall/update the USB driver in Device Manager
Format the flash drive immediately
Replace the workstation's motherboard
Disable USB in the BIOS
scenarios.why: Front-panel ports can be underpowered or loosely cabled, and a corrupt driver install affects one machine only. Testing a rear port plus a driver reinstall isolates port versus software. Formatting destroys the user's data to fix a connection problem.
scenarios.hint: Are all USB ports on a PC wired with the same power and controller path?

scenarios.title: The 169.254 address
scenarios.situation: A user cannot reach the internet or any network share. ipconfig shows 169.254.12.44 with no default gateway.
scenarios.prompt: What does this address tell you, and what is the first thing to check?
choices: It is an APIPA self-assigned address — the PC could not reach DHCP, so check the cable, switch port, and DHCP server
The DNS server is misconfigured — change DNS to a public resolver
Someone typed the wrong subnet mask — correct it manually
The ISP is down — call the provider
scenarios.why: 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA: Windows assigns it only when no DHCP server answers. No gateway means no routing, so the fix is at the DHCP layer — physical link, switch, then the DHCP service — not DNS.
scenarios.hint: Who normally hands this PC its address?

scenarios.title: Sizing the branch subnet
scenarios.situation: A new branch office will have about 50 networked devices on a single subnet. You want the smallest subnet that fits them, to conserve address space.
scenarios.prompt: Which subnet mask is the best fit?
scenarios.why: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 - 2 = 62 usable addresses, which covers 50 devices. A /27 gives only 30 (too small), while /25 and /24 waste space. Always subtract the network and broadcast addresses.
scenarios.hint: 2^5 - 2 = 30 and 2^6 - 2 = 62. Which side of 50 do you need to be on?

scenarios.title: IP works, names do not
scenarios.situation: From a workstation, ping 1.1.1.1 replies fine but no website name resolves — every domain fails while numeric IPs work.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fault, and how do you confirm it?
choices: DNS resolution is failing — check the DNS servers with ipconfig /all and test with nslookup
The Ethernet cable is damaged — replace it
The DHCP lease expired — release and renew
The firewall is blocking all traffic
scenarios.why: Reaching IPs but not names isolates the fault to DNS: connectivity is fine, name-to-IP translation is broken. ipconfig /all shows which DNS servers are configured; nslookup tests them directly.
scenarios.hint: Which service turns names into numbers?

scenarios.title: HTTP loads, HTTPS times out
scenarios.situation: Users can open http://intranet (port 80) but https://intranet (port 443) times out from the same workstations. The server itself is healthy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: Port 443 is blocked by a firewall rule between the clients and the server
DNS is failing for the hostname
The Wi-Fi password is wrong
DHCP has run out of leases
scenarios.why: One port working while another fails on the same host is the classic signature of a port-level block. HTTP on 80 passing proves DNS, DHCP, and cabling are fine; only 443 is filtered, so inspect firewall rules and ACLs.
scenarios.hint: Which port does the padlock use?

scenarios.title: The crowded-office slowdown
scenarios.situation: In a dense office, Wi-Fi on 2.4 GHz crawls at peak hours though the internet circuit is barely used. A survey shows neighboring networks stacked on the same channels.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best remediation?
choices: Move clients to 5 GHz where possible and place APs on the least-congested non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11)
Add a repeater on the same channel to boost the signal
Disable WPA2 to reduce encryption overhead
Crank every AP to maximum transmit power
scenarios.why: 2.4 GHz has only three non-overlapping channels, so dense offices suffer co-channel interference. 5 GHz offers many more channels and shorter range (less overlap), and proper channel planning beats raw power — more power just shouts over neighbors.
scenarios.hint: Which band gives you more non-overlapping channels to work with?

scenarios.title: The 120-meter run
scenarios.situation: A new copper Ethernet run of about 120 meters was just terminated. The switch shows no link light at either end, though the terminations test correctly for continuity.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong?
choices: The run exceeds the 100-meter limit for twisted-pair Ethernet — add a switch or re-route within spec
The IP address is wrong on the far end
Cat6a cable is required for any new run
Jumbo frames are not enabled
scenarios.why: Twisted-pair Ethernet (1000BASE-T and friends) is specified to 100 meters including patch cords. Beyond that, signal degradation kills the link regardless of perfect terminations. The fix is physical: shorten the run or add an intermediate switch.
scenarios.hint: What is the maximum specified length for a copper Ethernet run?

scenarios.title: The update boot loop
scenarios.situation: A Windows PC installed updates overnight and now reboots endlessly, never reaching the login screen. No new hardware was added.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best FIRST recovery step?
choices: Boot into the Windows Recovery Environment and use System Restore or Startup Repair
Reinstall Windows from scratch immediately
Replace the SSD
Disable UEFI in the firmware
scenarios.why: A boot loop right after updates points to a bad driver or update, not dead hardware. WinRE's System Restore rolls back to a restore point non-destructively — the least invasive path back to a working state before considering a reinstall.
scenarios.hint: What is the least destructive way back to yesterday?

scenarios.title: No space left on the server
scenarios.situation: A Linux server refuses updates with 'no space left on device', though the application data volume has plenty of room.
scenarios.prompt: How do you diagnose and fix it?
choices: Run df -h to find the full filesystem, then du to locate what is filling /var/log, and rotate or archive the logs
Delete files at random from /etc to make room
Add more RAM
Reboot and hope the filesystem recovers
scenarios.why: df -h shows which filesystem is full (often /var on a busy server), and du drills into directory sizes — logs that were never rotated are the usual culprit. Deleting blindly risks the OS; logrotate plus archiving fixes the cause.
scenarios.hint: Which directory grows on a busy server without anyone noticing?
evidence:
$ df -h
Filesystem  Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1    20G  20G   0G 100% /
$ du -sh /var/log
17G  /var/log

scenarios.title: Permission denied on your own script
scenarios.situation: You wrote a deployment script on Linux, but running ./deploy.sh fails with 'Permission denied' even though you own the file.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Add the execute bit with chmod +x deploy.sh
Always run everything with sudo instead
Move the script to /tmp where permissions do not matter
Rename it from .sh to .bash
scenarios.why: Ownership is not enough — Linux requires the execute permission bit to run a file directly. chmod +x adds it for the owner. Running as root or moving the file dodges the actual permission model instead of using it.
scenarios.hint: Of read, write, and execute — which one is missing?
evidence:
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 ops ops 214 Oct 3 09:12 deploy.sh
$ ./deploy.sh
bash: ./deploy.sh: Permission denied

scenarios.title: Disk pinned at 100%
scenarios.situation: A Windows PC is painfully slow. Task Manager shows disk usage pegged at 100% with no large file copies running, and the system is five years old.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best troubleshooting path?
choices: Check startup apps and background processes, then test drive health (SMART / chkdsk) for a failing disk
Install more RAM without investigating
Defragment the SSD
Permanently disable the antivirus
scenarios.why: Sustained 100% disk with no legitimate workload suggests either runaway processes or a dying drive retrying bad sectors. Checking SMART health distinguishes software bloat from hardware failure; defragging an SSD causes wear without helping.
scenarios.hint: What does sustained 100% disk with no big transfers suggest?

scenarios.title: Blue screens after a driver update
scenarios.situation: A workstation started blue-screening twice a day right after a GPU driver update. Nothing else changed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first step?
choices: Boot into Safe Mode and roll the driver back to the previous version
Buy a replacement GPU
Reinstall Windows
Ignore it — blue screens fix themselves
scenarios.why: The timeline implicates the driver: crashes began immediately after the change. Safe Mode loads a minimal driver set so you can roll back cleanly. Replacing hardware or reinstalling the OS skips the obvious, reversible cause.
scenarios.hint: What changed right before the crashes started?

scenarios.title: The process that will not die
scenarios.situation: A hung Linux application ignores a normal kill command and keeps holding a port your service needs.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct escalation?
choices: Send SIGKILL with kill -9 as a last resort, after SIGTERM (kill 15) failed
Immediately reboot the server
Delete the application's binary
Send SIGHUP and walk away
scenarios.why: SIGTERM (15) asks politely and lets the process clean up; SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored and is the guaranteed escalation. Rebooting the whole server for one hung process is disproportionate, and deleting binaries does not stop a running process.
scenarios.hint: Which signal can a process neither catch nor ignore?

scenarios.title: The urgent account email
scenarios.situation: You receive an email that looks like it is from your bank: 'Unusual activity — verify your account within 24 hours or it will be locked.' The logo looks right but the sender address is odd.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Do not click the link — report the message, then visit the bank's site by typing its address yourself
Click the link quickly to check whether it is real
Reply asking if the email is legitimate
Forward it to coworkers as a warning
scenarios.why: Urgency plus a link is the classic phishing formula; logos are trivially copied. The safe verification path never uses the attacker's link — navigate to the known-good site manually. Replying confirms your address is active to the attacker.
scenarios.hint: How would you reach your bank without touching that link?

scenarios.title: The ransom note
scenarios.situation: You open your PC to find a ransom note: files are renamed with a strange extension and a timer demands payment in cryptocurrency.
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct FIRST actions?
choices: Disconnect from the network immediately, do not pay, and restore from a known-clean backup after containment
Pay the ransom right away to beat the timer
Keep working — maybe only some files are affected
Delete the ransom note so nobody panics
scenarios.why: Isolation stops the ransomware spreading to shares and backups; paying funds crime with no guarantee of decryption. Recovery comes from clean, tested backups — which is why backup verification matters before an incident, not during one.
scenarios.hint: What is the first thing the malware wants you NOT to do?

scenarios.title: One password everywhere
scenarios.situation: A colleague uses the same password for work email, banking, and a hobby forum. The forum just announced a breach.
scenarios.prompt: What should they do?
choices: Switch to unique passwords everywhere with a password manager, and enable MFA on every account that offers it
Change only the forum password
Pick one stronger password and keep reusing it
Rely on security questions instead
scenarios.why: Breached credentials are tried automatically against banks and email (credential stuffing). Unique passwords contain each breach, and MFA blocks logins even when a password leaks. A password manager makes uniqueness practical.
scenarios.hint: If one key opens every door, what happens when it is copied?

scenarios.title: The stolen laptop
scenarios.situation: A laptop with customer spreadsheets is stolen from a car. It had a login password but no encryption.
scenarios.prompt: What control would have protected the data?
choices: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault) plus remote-wipe capability
Storing files in an obscurely named folder
Hoping the thief only wants the hardware
A screensaver password
scenarios.why: A login password only guards a running OS — the thief can remove the drive and read it directly. Full-disk encryption makes the entire drive unreadable without the key, which is why it is the baseline for mobile devices.
scenarios.hint: What protects the data when the thief removes the drive?

scenarios.title: The stranger at the badge door
scenarios.situation: Someone you do not recognize follows closely behind you through a badge-controlled door, smiling and carrying a large box.
scenarios.prompt: What should you do?
choices: Politely decline to hold the door and direct them to check in at reception
Hold the door — it would be rude not to
Ignore them and keep walking
Lend them your badge for the day
scenarios.why: Tailgating bypasses every technical access control with social pressure. The box is a classic prop. A polite redirect to reception enforces the badge policy without confrontation — physical security depends on people, not just readers.
scenarios.hint: What is the badge reader actually enforcing?

scenarios.title: Coffee-shop email
scenarios.situation: You need to check work email from a café's open Wi-Fi network with no password.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safest approach?
choices: Connect through the company VPN before doing anything sensitive
It is fine — the sites use HTTPS anyway
Temporarily disable the firewall for better speed
Use WPS to connect faster
scenarios.why: Open Wi-Fi broadcasts your traffic to everyone nearby; not all traffic is encrypted and portals can be spoofed. A VPN encrypts everything between you and the office, neutralizing local eavesdropping regardless of what the café network does.
scenarios.hint: Who else can read unencrypted traffic on an open network?

scenarios.title: The motherboard swap
scenarios.situation: You are replacing a motherboard on a repair bench. The room has carpet, and it is a dry winter day.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct ESD precaution?
choices: Wear an anti-static wrist strap connected to a mat, with the PSU unplugged
Work in socks on the carpet — comfort first
Leave the PC plugged in so it stays grounded while you work
Handle the board by its pins for a firm grip
scenarios.why: Electrostatic discharge you cannot feel can destroy chips. A wrist strap and mat keep you and the components at equal potential; the PSU must be unplugged so no live power is present. Carpet and dry air maximize static buildup.
scenarios.hint: What invisible charge kills chips before you feel it?

scenarios.title: Friday-afternoon patching
scenarios.situation: A critical patch must go on a production server. Your manager says 'just do it now' on a Friday afternoon.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct procedure?
choices: Follow change control: approval, a maintenance window, testing, and a documented backout plan
Apply it immediately — urgency overrides process
Patch quietly and mention it Monday if it works
Skip testing to save time
scenarios.why: Change management exists for exactly this moment: untested Friday changes become weekend outages with no rollback. An approved window, a tested backout plan, and stakeholder notice turn a gamble into a controlled operation.
scenarios.hint: What do you need at 2 AM if the patch breaks everything?

scenarios.title: Drives full of customer PII
scenarios.situation: The company is retiring ten hard drives that held customer records. Policy requires the data be unrecoverable.
scenarios.prompt: Which disposal method complies?
choices: Physical destruction (shredding/crushing) or degaussing per the media-sanitization policy
Quick-format each drive
Throw them in the dumpster — they are old
Delete the files and empty the recycle bin
scenarios.why: Formatting and file deletion only remove pointers; forensic tools recover the data easily. For PII on retired media, only destruction or degaussing (for magnetic media) guarantees unrecoverability, with a certificate of destruction for the audit trail.
scenarios.hint: Can formatted data be recovered?

scenarios.title: The fix only you know
scenarios.situation: You just solved a bizarre printer issue after two hours of digging. The ticket is still open.
scenarios.prompt: What should you do before closing it?
choices: Document the symptoms, cause, and fix in the ticket and the knowledge base
Keep it in your head — job security
Mention it to one coworker in passing
Close the ticket silently to keep metrics clean
scenarios.why: Undocumented fixes die with your memory and the next person burns the same two hours. Tickets plus a searchable knowledge base turn one fix into an organizational asset and prove the work during audits.
scenarios.hint: Who fixes this at 3 AM next month when you are on vacation?

scenarios.title: Proving the backup works
scenarios.situation: A department keeps one copy of its project files on an external drive under someone's desk.
scenarios.prompt: What backup strategy should you recommend?
choices: 3-2-1: three copies, two different media, one offsite — with periodic test restores
One USB copy is enough if it is a big drive
RAID on the workstation counts as the backup
Cloud sync alone, never tested
scenarios.why: 3-2-1 survives drive failure, theft, fire, and ransomware; RAID is availability, not backup, and sync copies corruption instantly. Only a test restore proves recoverability — untested backups are wishes.
scenarios.hint: What is the only proof a backup actually works?

scenarios.title: The toner spill
scenarios.situation: A toner cartridge burst inside a laser printer, coating the area in fine black powder.
scenarios.prompt: How do you clean it safely?
choices: Use a toner-rated vacuum with proper filtration and wear a dust mask — never a standard vacuum
Use the regular office vacuum — faster
Wipe it with a damp cloth and bare hands only
Blow it out with compressed air
scenarios.why: Toner particles are extremely fine: standard vacuums blow them through the exhaust or risk static ignition, and compressed air just spreads them. A toner-rated (HEPA/ESD-safe) vacuum plus a mask is the safe procedure.
scenarios.hint: What do ultra-fine toner particles do inside a standard vacuum?

scenarios.title: Read the ipconfig
scenarios.situation: A user cannot reach anything on the network. You run ipconfig on their PC.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and the correct first action?
choices: DHCP failure — verify the physical link, then check the switch port and DHCP server scope
Set a static DNS server and retry
Replace the network adapter
Run ipconfig /flushdns
scenarios.why: 169.254.x.x with no gateway is APIPA: the client never got a DHCP offer. Flushing DNS or setting static DNS treats a symptom of a lower-layer problem — start at the physical link and work up to the DHCP service.
scenarios.hint: Which layer hands out addresses — and which layer is actually broken?
evidence:
Ethernet adapter Local Area Connection:
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . : 169.254.12.44
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . : 255.255.0.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . : 
   Media State . . . . . . . . : connected

scenarios.title: Read the tracert
scenarios.situation: Users report the internet is down. From the router you run a tracert to 8.8.8.8.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the fault, and what do you do next?
choices: The trace dies at hop 3 — the problem is at or beyond the ISP handoff; verify the WAN link, then escalate to the provider
Reinstall the web browser on user PCs
Change the office DNS servers
Switch the Wi-Fi channel
scenarios.why: Hops 1–2 (local) answer, then everything times out: traffic leaves your equipment and dies upstream. That localizes the fault past your demarc — check the WAN interface status, then open a ticket with the ISP with the trace as evidence.
scenarios.hint: Which hop is the last one that answers you?
evidence:
1    <1 ms   192.168.1.1
2     8 ms   10.20.30.1
3     *        *        *     Request timed out.
4     *        *        *     Request timed out.

scenarios.title: Read the ls -l
scenarios.situation: Teammates report they cannot read a shared report file on the Linux file server, though the owner opens it fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the fix?
choices: Group and others have no read permission — grant read with chmod g+r,o+r (e.g. 644)
Change ownership to root
Move the file to another directory
Reboot the file server
scenarios.why: -rw-rw---- gives read/write to owner and group only, nothing to others. If the teammates are not in the file's group, they are locked out. Adding the read bit (644 is the standard for shared readable files) fixes it without touching ownership.
scenarios.hint: Which of the three permission triplets applies to the teammates?

scenarios.title: Read the rule list
scenarios.situation: After a firewall change, HTTPS to the company portal broke but HTTP still works. You pull the rule list.
scenarios.prompt: Which rule is the problem and what is the fix?
choices: Rule 3 denies TCP 443 — reorder or edit it to allow 443 to the portal server
Rule 1 is wrong — HTTP should be denied
The DNS rule is missing
All rules are fine — replace the firewall
scenarios.why: Firewalls process rules top-down and stop at the first match: rule 3's explicit deny of 443 hits before any later allow. HTTP on port 80 is unaffected, which matches the symptom exactly. Fix the rule order or the rule itself.
scenarios.hint: In what order does a firewall evaluate rules — and what does it do at the first match?
evidence:
1  ALLOW  tcp/80   -> 10.0.5.10
2  ALLOW  tcp/53   -> any
3  DENY   tcp/443  -> any
4  ALLOW  tcp/443  -> 10.0.5.10

scenarios.title: Read the system log
scenarios.situation: A server has been freezing for a week. You check the system log around the freeze times.
scenarios.prompt: What is failing and what do you do?
choices: The disk on PhysicalDrive1 is throwing I/O errors — back it up immediately and replace the drive
Defragment the drive this weekend
Update the antivirus definitions
Ignore warnings until an actual error appears
scenarios.why: Repeated disk I/O errors clustered at freeze times are a failing drive signature, not a software issue. Errors (not just warnings) on the same device mean imminent failure: back up now, then replace — defragging a dying disk accelerates its death.
scenarios.hint: Warnings whisper, errors shout. What device keeps appearing?
evidence:
08:12:04  WARNING  disk: retry on \.\PhysicalDrive1
08:12:09  ERROR    disk: I/O error on \.\PhysicalDrive1
08:12:15  ERROR    disk: I/O error on \.\PhysicalDrive1
08:12:31  SYSTEM   freeze detected

scenarios.title: Read the site survey
scenarios.situation: Users complain about Wi-Fi drops in a conference room. Your survey of 2.4 GHz shows the room's AP on channel 6, fighting neighboring networks.
scenarios.prompt: Which channel should the AP move to?
choices: Channel 11 — the clearest of the three non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11)
Channel 3 — it looks half-empty
Channel 6 — stay put and raise power
Any channel — Auto will sort it out
scenarios.why: On 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap; a 'half-empty' channel 3 overlaps both 1 and 6 and makes things worse for everyone. Channel 11 is the only non-overlapping channel with real clearance in this survey.
scenarios.hint: Which three 2.4 GHz channels do not overlap each other?
evidence:
ch 1 : ██████████ heavy
ch 3 : ████ moderate
ch 6 : ████████ heavy (our AP)
ch 11: █ light

lessons.title: CompTIA Core (A+ Track) — Core concepts
concepts: Memory must match the board: DDR generations are not interchangeable — different notch positions and voltages — and dual-channel mode needs matched pairs in the slots the manual specifies. Check the board's slot map before buying.

Storage interfaces set your ceiling: an NVMe drive is only faster if the slot, keying, and protocol support it. A 2.5-inch SATA SSD is the safe universal upgrade for older machines still on spinning disks.
Power problems masquerade as everything else: random reboots and shutdowns under load point at the PSU or thermals first. Verify wattage headroom and cooling before blaming the motherboard.
Mobile devices fail differently: a swollen battery is a safety hazard with puncture and fire risk — power down, do not charge, and follow hazardous-material disposal procedures.

Printers are mechanical: most jams come from worn pickup rollers or wrong paper-type settings, and laser print defects map to a specific stage of the imaging process — charge, expose, develop, transfer, fuse.

Operational procedures protect you: change management with backout plans, ESD precautions, safety steps like disconnecting power, documentation, and the structured methodology — identify, theorize, test, act, verify, document.

example.walkthrough: -H asks the drive for its overall SMART health verdict (PASSED or FAILED). The second command pulls raw attributes so you can see reallocated sector counts and power-on hours before deciding whether to clone the drive preemptively.

pitfalls: Common trap: seating a single RAM stick and expecting dual-channel — dual-channel needs a matched pair in the board's designated slots.
Common trap: forcing a DDR module into the wrong slot — the notch is keyed per generation, so never force it.
Common trap: skipping the PSU wattage check when adding a GPU — an underrated supply causes 'random' crashes under load.
Common trap: treating every incident as break-fix — undocumented changes make the next failure harder to diagnose.

simulations.title: The fstab that won't boot
simulations.brief: The machine drops to emergency shell on boot. /etc/fstab has 2 bugs in 6 lines.

steps.config:
# /etc/fstab
UUID=aaa1 / ext4 defaults 0 1
UUID=bbb2 /data ext4 defaults 0 2
/dev/sdc1 /backup ext4 nofail 0 2
tmpfs /tmp tmpfs defaults 0 0
# mount -a to test

issues.description: /data's filesystem UUID bbb2 doesn't match any attached disk — boot waits, then fails into emergency shell.
issues.fix: Correct the UUID (blkid) or add nofail if /data is optional.

issues.description: /dev/sdc1 is a device name, not a UUID — device names can reorder across boots; without nofail a missing disk halts boot.
issues.fix: Use UUID= plus nofail for removable/optional disks.

simulations.debrief: fstab is a boot contract: wrong UUIDs and bare device names turn reboots into emergency shells. Validate with mount -a before you reboot.

Electrostatic discharge you cannot feel can destroy chips. A wrist strap and mat keep you and the components at equal potential; the PSU must be unplugged so no live power is present.
Common trap: leave the PC plugged in so it stays grounded while you work.
Media sanitization: for PII on retired media, only destruction or degaussing (for magnetic media) guarantees unrecoverability, with a certificate of destruction for the audit trail.
Linux permissions: ownership is not enough — Linux requires the execute permission bit to run a file directly. chmod +x adds it for the owner.
Thermal events before shutdown mean the CPU is overheating and triggering its protection cutoff. Puncturing or freezing it risks thermal runaway.
System Restore: winRE's System Restore rolls back to a restore point non-destructively — the least invasive path back to a working state before considering a reinstall.

DHCP: HTTP on 80 passing proves DNS, DHCP, and cabling are fine; only 443 is filtered, so inspect firewall rules and ACLs. 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA: Windows assigns it only when no DHCP server answers.

SIGTERM (15) asks politely and lets the process clean up; SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored and is the guaranteed escalation. Rebooting the whole server for one hung process is disproportionate, and deleting binaries does not stop…

Repeated disk I/O errors clustered at freeze times are a failing drive signature, not a software issue. Errors (not just warnings) on the same device mean imminent failure: back up now, then replace — defragging a dying disk accelerates…

Toner particles are extremely fine: standard vacuums blow them through the exhaust or risk static ignition, and compressed air just spreads them. A toner-rated (HEPA/ESD-safe) vacuum plus a mask is the safe procedure.

On 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap; a 'half-empty' channel 3 overlaps both 1 and 6 and makes things worse for everyone. Channel 11 is the only non-overlapping channel with real clearance in this survey.

Ghosting on a laser printer means the drum is not fully discharging between rotations or toner is low, so a faint residual image transfers again. It is a consumable problem, not software — the driver cannot cause a repeated physical image.
